name: Middle Clarence Bandjalang
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: midd1357 (Middle Clarence Bandjalang) is not in the catalog under this key; the same lect is coded in the catalog as band1339 'Bandjalang' (weight-sensitive (tentative), quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2: Hayes 1980 pp.108-109/170 fn.2 and StressTyp2-carried Hammond 1986:193,195, all second-hand on Crowley 1978). this search of works with stress in the title's one item, Hammond 1986 NLLT 4 (DOI 10.1007/BF00133844), is relevant -- the Springer landing page (opened via direct download) lists Crowley 1978 The Middle Clarence Dialects of Bandjalang in its references and StressTyp2 carries its Bandjalang sentences from pp.193/195 ('Main stress is generally initial, secondary stress on long vowels'; 'Words with main stress on the second vowel are only optional variants') -- but it is paywalled (Springer USD 39.95; Unpaywall closed; S2 closed; not on Hammond's Arizona/GitHub pages; CORE/BASE/IA Scholar blocked), so nothing in it was read first-hand: access = paywalled, priority medium (it is a secondary analysis whose Bandjalang content is already carried verbatim by StressTyp2). The primary that would settle the classification, Crowley 1978 (AIAS, 492 pp; not among the works with stress in the title), remains unreachable: archive.org middleclarencedi0000crow is lending/printdisabled only (metadata re-downloaded; search-inside 'Item not available'; priority HIGH for acquisition (library or IA borrow). Best first-hand statement actually read this search of works with stress in the title is Sharpe 1997 (PL C-136) p.372, already held by the project: stress is initial unless a non-initial syllable has a long vowel ('By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed'), corroborating the band1339 coding (initial, long-vowel-sensitive) without superseding it; Wikipedia's Stress section (downloaded wikitext) attributes the same quantity-sensitive picture to Sharpe 2005:180 (LINCOM grammar, closed). Cunningham 1969:75 (Yugumbir, sister dialect, held by the project) gives 'first syllable.. or the first long syllable if such is present'.org/Wikipedia APIs and direct downloads.

The sentence closes section 1.4 on transcription conventions, immediately before '2. VOWEL SHIFTS RELIABLY NOTED IN THE DIFFERENT DIALECTS'. Corroborating passages in the same paper, verified:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress is on the first syllable; when stress is heard elsewhere in the word, that syllable is one with a long vowel (vowel length attracts stress). The Waalubal-specific version carried from Crowley 1978 by Hayes 1980:109 / Goedemans 1998 / StressTyp2: main stress on the initial syllable unless the first vowel is short and the second long, in which case on the second; Sharpe 1998:14,16 (Yugambeh, 'as are the other dialects') states it as: the first syllable is stressed except when a long vowel elsewhere in the word takes the primary stress; long vowels are stressed, otherwise the first syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sharpe 1997 is silent. Second-hand for Waalubal: Hayes 1980:170 fn.2 and Hammond 1986:193 (via StressTyp2) place secondary stress on long vowels; Sharpe 1998:16 adds that two long vowels (almost) never occur in a row, and Sharpe 1997:373 notes vowel shortening forced by the stress pattern.
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually' hedges the initial default. Second-hand: Hammond 1986:195 (via StressTyp2) says words with main stress on the second vowel are only optional variants; StressTyp2/Rice 1992 (Gidabal, pattern 'Exceptional (Waalubal)') reports free variation in L-H disyllables (djuluːn ~ djuˈluːn).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, from wordlist citation forms across the Yugambeh-Bundjalung dialect chain (Sharpe's own Western Bundjalung data plus Crowley's Wahlubal/Wehlubal and the Geytenbeeks' Gidhabal); the sentence is framed as a transcription convention and is indirect, so confidence is medium. The Middle-Clarence-specific primary description (Crowley 1978) was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog band1339 is the FAMILY node 'Bandjalangic', not a language: the catalog's existing weight-sensitive tier unit keyed band1339 'Bandjalang (Waalubal)' (the StressTyp2 entry for this language, WALS bwa, Crowley 1978) actually describes the Waalubal dialect [waal1238] of Middle Clarence Bandjalang [midd1357], i.e. this language. The quoted Sharpe 1997 statement is chain-wide (Yugambeh-Bundjalung) and explicitly built on Crowley's Wahlubal/Wehlubal (Middle Clarence), the Geytenbeeks' Gidhabal [gida1240] and Sharpe's own Western Bundjalung (Tabulam/Baryulgil = Middle Clarence) data; Sharpe 1998's more direct wording is for Yugambeh [yugu1249, Tweed-Albert]. Cunningham 1969 = Yugumbir [yugu1249]; Livingstone 1892 = Minjangbal [minj1242] (Glottolog files it under midd1357 but it is Tweed-Albert and is silent on stress).

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by a linguist who worked on the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung dialect chain, explicitly covering Crowley's (Middle Clarence) analysis: the default stressed syllable is the first, and where stress is perceived elsewhere than the first syllable the stressed syllable contains a long vowel -- i.e. initial stress, attracted to a long vowel (CVV-sensitive); it says nothing about which of several long vowels wins or about the disyllabic L-H variation reported by Hayes/Hammond. It is weaker than the (unreached) Crowley 1978 primary and than the StressTyp2-carried Hayes 1980 / Hammond 1986 rule, so it should be read as a corroborating first-hand statement, not as a new deciding source. Consistent with the sister-dialect primaries held by the project: Cunningham 1969:75 (Yugumbir) 'Stress occurs on the first syllable of the word, or on the first long syllable if such is present', and Hayes 1980:109 (carrying Crowley 1978 for Waalubal) 'the mirror image stress pattern [of Yapese] is reported for.. the Waalubal dialect of Bandjalang', fn. 2 p.170 'Banjalang also ha[s] secondary stress, which falls on long vowels'.

new_statements.quote: 4. ACCENTUATION Generally speaking syllables containing long vowels tend to be accentu¬ ated . 'ba:banj 'grandmother' baba'ra: 'on top' ba'ga: 'shield' ba'gargir 'coral tree' bai'ja:nj 'today' wu'dje: 'you' 'wu:dja 'you' mumu'na: 'that' In words of short vowels the main accent tends to fall on the initial syllable, with a secondary accent on the penultimate. 'gale 'this' 'babargam 'over there' 'babargam'wanbi 'may become increased' [...] 'wadjug!djargan 'his mother-in-law' Case and verbal enclitics do not affect accent patterns except occasional ly when they have a long vowel or are of more than one syllable. 'beigal 'man' > 'beigalu (operative) > beigal'na: (active possessive)

Compatible with the statements held by the project (Sharpe 1997:372: the syllable perceived as stressed off the first syllable has a long vowel; Crowley 1978:21 Waalubal: initial primary stress, optional shift to a long second syllable, secondary stress on long vowels) in type: default-initial, long vowels attract prominence = weight-sensitive. Adds for the Casino dialect: (i) long-vowel attraction stated for any position, not only the second syllable; (ii) a positional secondary accent on the PENULTIMATE in all-short words (Crowley instead gives length-based secondary stress and says nothing about all-short words beyond initial primary); (iii) enclitic behav…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Casino-dialect Bandjalang (Smythe, 1940s): syllables with long vowels attract the accent, whatever their position (baba'ra:, mumu'na:, wu'dje: final; 'ba:banj, 'wu:dja initial). In words with only short vowels the main accent is on the first syllable and a secondary accent on the penultimate ('babargam'wanbi). Case and verbal enclitics normally leave the pattern unchanged, but a long-vowel or polysyllabic enclitic can carry accent ('beigal > 'beigalu but beigal'na:). All rules hedged with 'generally speaking' / 'tends to'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In all-short-vowel words a secondary accent on the penultimate syllable (positional), e.g. 'babargam'wanbi; nothing said about secondary accent in words with long vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedges 'generally speaking', 'tend(s) to'; enclitics 'occasionally' affect the pattern when they contain a long vowel or more than one syllable (beigal'na:); ba'gargir 'coral tree' is written with non-initial accent and no length mark in the scanned (length mark possibly lost).
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley 1978 ch.2 describes Waalubal (Tabulam speaker Mrs Ethel Walker) with data also from Biriin and Baryulgil speakers = Glottolog midd1357's Waalubal/Biriin/Baryulgil dialects; Smythe's appendix describes the Casino dialect (midd1357 'Casino'); Geytenbeek & Geytenbeek 1971 describes Gidabal (Woodenbong) = Glottolog cond1242, not midd1357; Sharpe 2005 covers the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung chain (Glottolog files it under twee1234).

new_statements.quote: 7. STRESS There is not a very strong difference auditorily between stressed and unstressed syllables in Waalubal, and the stress rules that can be set up seem to be affected by a certain fluidity in application. [...] vowel length and position in a word of a syl lable are the main determ¬ inants of which syllable will be stressed. Primary stress goes on the first syl lable of a word, or if the second syl lable contains a long vowel, stress is optionally shifted to th i s sy I I ab I e . If the first syllable has primary stress and the word contains a syllable with a long vowel, this receives secondary stress, for example: bandag ba : pb i n i [...] 8. DISTINCTIVE FEATURES

new_statements.rule_in_words: Waalubal: weak, somewhat variable stress. Primary stress on the first syllable; if the second syllable has a long vowel, primary stress may optionally move to it. When the first syllable keeps primary stress, a later long-vowel syllable gets secondary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Long-vowel syllables receive secondary stress when primary stress stays on the first syllable (p.21).
new_statements.exceptions: Optional shift to a long second syllable; 'a certain fluidity in application'; weak auditory difference. Unstressed a/e centralised or reduced to schwa (pp.15-16, footnote on bani).

Springer landing page (opened): reference list includes "Crowley, T.: 1978, The Middle Clarence Dialects of Bandjalang, Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies, Canberra"; conclusion preview: "ROB feet enable us to capture the fact that in certain positions (nonhead positions) under certain types of iteration or scanning (ROB types), heavy syllables are treated just like light syllables."
